newsitem.title: ITALY: Parliament can help speed Italian rate cut - Ciampi.
newsitem.headline: Parliament can help speed Italian rate cut - Ciampi.

text.p: Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi on Thursday urged parliament to speed the government's 1997 budget into law and pave the way for a cut in official interest rates.
Ciampi told the Upper House (Senate) that the recently unveiled budget, which aims to slash 62.5 trillion lire off next year's public sector deficit, has already helped Italian market rates to ease.
"It is now necessary to consolidate with facts...and carry on with what has already been announced," Ciampi said.
He said the budget had made no provisions for lower interest rates to add to the "credibility" of the package.

"But the prize (of a rate cut), if we deserve it, will be a sign of our success, of fully recovered credibility, the turning point for re-balancing government books, a sure support for re-launching production and investment," he told the Senate.

He said Italian market rates were at their lowest level for decades. A full percentage point fall in interest rates would bring the government savings of seven trillion lire on debt interest repayments in the first year, Ciampi said.
Once the cut had fully worked its way into the system, it would bring annual savings of 20 trillion lire a year, he said.
Ciampi said a tough budget was needed to ensure Italy became a founder member of European economic and monetary union (EMU) from its planned launch in 1999.

"We could certainly enter the single currency in a second phase, the gates will not be shut. But it would not be the same thing," Ciampi said. "We are today facing one of those moments which weigh heavily on the future of a country."
In order to get Italy into shape for EMU, the government at the last minute doubled the size of the budget.

"The determination within the European Union to adhere to the EMU timetable has strengthened. At the same time, single EU countries are making more intensive convergence efforts to meet the terms of the Maastricht Treaty," Ciampi told the Senate.
He said the government had decided to up the tempo to reach the Maastricht goals because it perceived an improvement in recent months in the European economy.

"Worries that the slowdown in output which we have seen since the second half of 1995, could turn into a recession, seem to be disappearing," Ciampi said, adding that the International Monetary Fund and European Commission had said the same thing.
The budget is being examined at committee stage by the lower chamber of parliament. Both houses must approve the package by the end of the year. -- Crispian Balmer, Rome newsroom +396 6782501
